questions.prompt: What is identity resolution, as used in Lesson 1's Data Cloud design for Meridian Outfitters?
options: Matching and merging records that represent the same real-world customer across multiple source systems
Deleting a customer's record permanently once their account closes
A Salesforce feature that automatically merges three production orgs into one
A method for compressing years of order history into a Big Object
questions.explain: Identity resolution matches and merges records representing the same real-world customer across the three regional orgs and the new commerce platform, without requiring any of them to migrate or merge data first.
questions.distractorExplain: Automatically merging the three production orgs describes full org consolidation, which Lesson 1 specifically avoided for the nine-month launch — identity resolution works across the existing orgs without migrating or merging their underlying data.

questions.prompt: Alder Trust Bank's design uses deterministic Shield encryption on the account-balance field instead of the stronger non-deterministic scheme used on the SSN field. Why?
options: Deterministic encryption is always required by banking regulators
The compliance team needs exact-match filtering on balances, which non-deterministic encryption would block
Non-deterministic encryption cannot be applied to numeric fields
Account balances are not considered sensitive data
questions.explain: The choice matches each field's protection scheme to how it actually needs to be used operationally — the compliance team's reporting depends on exact-match filtering that non-deterministic encryption would break.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about Brightwell Health Network's consent-record design from Lesson 3.
options: Consent is modeled as its own record per patient per channel, not a single checkbox
Step-up authentication adds an extra identity check for viewing lab results, beyond standard login
The EHR remains the system of record for clinical data; Salesforce is the engagement layer
Shield Platform Encryption alone is sufficient to guarantee only the correct care team sees a patient's record
questions.explain: Consent lives in its own auditable record per channel, step-up authentication gates the highest-risk actions, and the EHR stays authoritative for clinical data. Encryption alone does not control who can see a record inside the application — that's the sharing model's job, not encryption's.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: Carrow Equipment's design uses ________ (external objects) to query SAP's pricing and inventory live, rather than replicating that data into Salesforce.
questions.explain: Salesforce Connect queries SAP in real time through external objects, which is the right tool when freshness at the moment of use matters more than query performance or offline availability.

questions.prompt: Match each persona in the Public Sector Case Management design to what they can actually see.
left: Child welfare case subject in specific legal circumstances
right: May be legally prevented from ever seeing that a case exists at all
Only their own household's application status, never another citizen's
Only cases explicitly assigned to them
Their team's caseload, not the whole department
questions.explain: Caseworkers see only assigned cases, supervisors see their team's caseload, citizens see only their own household's status through sharing sets, and in child welfare specifically a case can be legally invisible to a given person entirely — a stronger requirement than ordinary restricted visibility.

questions.prompt: Put these in the order Nimbus Mobile's design handles a regional outage, from detection to agent alert.
items: Network-monitoring system detects a regional outage
The monitoring system publishes an event
A subscriber on the Salesforce side fans the event out
Every currently-active agent handling that region receives the alert within seconds
questions.explain: This is an event-driven broadcast, not a routed Case: detection triggers a published event, which a subscriber fans out to every relevant active agent, rather than waiting for one-to-one routing through Omni-Channel.

questions.prompt: Why does Fenwick State University's design extend EDA's existing affiliation and relationship objects for advisor-student assignment instead of building a parallel custom object?
options: EDA does not allow any custom objects to be added
Custom objects are against Salesforce's platform terms of service
Building a parallel object would duplicate relationship modeling EDA already provides and lose existing reporting/tooling built on the standard shape
FERPA requires all student data to live in a single object
questions.explain: EDA's affiliation and relationship objects already model exactly this kind of relationship — building a parallel structure duplicates that work and loses whatever tooling already understands the standard shape.

questions.prompt: In the Full Mock Review Board format (Lesson 8), what does the "opening" portion of a presentation need to do?
options: Jump directly into the architecture diagram to save time
List every Salesforce product used in the design
Ask the panel what they already know about the scenario
Restate the business problem and its key constraints before presenting the solution
questions.explain: The opening restates the business problem and its key constraints before the solution is shown, demonstrating the candidate understood what was actually asked.
questions.distractorExplain: Jumping straight into the diagram skips the step a panel is specifically listening for — demonstrating the candidate understood the problem — even if the diagram itself turns out to be correct.

questions.prompt: A panelist asks why Meridian Outfitters didn't just merge the three regional orgs as leadership requested. What is the strongest response?
options: Name the actual business commitment (unified profile, real-time inventory, deadline) and explain why a full merge was the higher-risk path given the deadline and data-quality issues, while keeping consolidation open as a later step
Insist leadership's wording was a mistake and should be ignored
Claim org consolidation is technically impossible on the Salesforce platform
Avoid answering and move to the next topic
questions.explain: This response names the underlying business goal, the specific risk factors that ruled out a literal merge on this timeline, and the fact that consolidation remains possible later — the defensible pattern Lesson 1 and Lesson 8 both teach.

questions.prompt: Select every case study in Chapter 1 that centers on a sharing/visibility decision stricter than standard role-hierarchy sharing.
options: Carrow Equipment (dealer peer-to-peer isolation)
Public Sector Case Management (need-to-know, cross-program consent)
Fenwick State University (FERPA-driven advisor-only access)
Nimbus Mobile (Omni-Channel skills-based routing)
questions.explain: Carrow, the Public Sector case, and Fenwick State all center on sharing models stricter than role hierarchy. Nimbus Mobile's Omni-Channel routing is a work-distribution mechanism, not a sharing/visibility decision.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: in Brightwell Health Network's design, ________ remains the system of record for clinical data, while Salesforce serves as the engagement layer.
questions.explain: Salesforce doesn't try to own diagnosis history or the authoritative medical record — it receives what it needs from the EHR to support appointment reminders, care-plan tracking, and messaging.

questions.prompt: What are the three categories Lesson 9 teaches for sorting a scenario prompt's details?
options: High, medium, and low priority
Explicit requirements, implied constraints, and decorative detail
Technical, delivery, and business risk
Data, integration, and security domains
questions.explain: These three categories — stated directly, following by necessary inference, or just context — are the sorting scheme Lesson 9 teaches for a first read-through of any scenario.

questions.prompt: What is the "removal test" from Lesson 9 used for?
options: Deciding whether a risk is high or low impact
Checking whether an assumption's consequence was stated
Asking whether removing or changing a detail would change what a correct design looks like, to tell an implied constraint from decorative detail
Determining which blueprint artifact to present first
questions.explain: If removing a detail wouldn't change any design decision, it was decorative; if it would allow a materially different design, it was doing real constraining work.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about stating assumptions explicitly, per Lesson 10.
options: A silent guess and a stated assumption carry the same risk if they turn out wrong
A strong assumptions section names the specific consequence if the assumption is wrong
The four assumption categories include scale/volume, budget/timeline, existing technology investment, and risk appetite
Writing an assumption down invites the panel to question it directly
questions.explain: A silent guess that turns out wrong looks like a mistake, while the same guess stated openly looks like a documented, reasonable judgment call — the risk is not the same, which is exactly Lesson 10's point.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: Lesson 11 sorts risks along two axes: ________ and impact.
questions.explain: Sorting risks by how likely they are and how bad they'd be if they occurred is what separates risks that must visibly shape the design from ones that only need a brief acknowledgment.

questions.prompt: Match each risk category from Lesson 11 to its definition.
right: Whether the organization, customers, or reputation are harmed even if the build succeeds
Whether the solution works as designed
Whether the team can build and ship it in the given timeframe
questions.explain: Technical risk is about whether the solution works; delivery risk is about whether the team can build and ship it on time; business risk is about harm to the organization or customers even if the build succeeds technically.

questions.prompt: Put these four blueprint artifacts from Lesson 12 in the order this course presents them.
questions.explain: The blueprint moves from the entities and their relationships, to how systems exchange data, to who can see and do what, to each persona's actual access path — four connected artifacts, not one diagram repeated four times.

questions.prompt: Why does Lesson 13 warn against "strawmanning" a rejected alternative?
options: Because every rejected alternative must eventually be chosen instead
Because strawmanning is formally banned under certification rules
Because rejected alternatives should never be mentioned in a presentation
Because misrepresenting the alternative's real strengths to make the chosen design look better reads as evasive, even when the final recommendation is correct
questions.explain: A panel can tell the difference between a fairly considered and honestly rejected alternative and a caricatured one designed just to make the chosen answer look better by comparison.

questions.prompt: Per Lesson 10's categories, which of these is a "risk-appetite" assumption?
options: Assuming Alder Trust Bank would rather accept a slower onboarding flow than relax its two-approver rule
Assuming a specific number of concurrent portal users
Assuming the client already has Shield licensed
Assuming a dealer network has some identity provider in place
questions.explain: This is a judgment about how a client is likely to prioritize a trade-off based on their described context, which is exactly what a risk-appetite assumption fills in.

questions.prompt: According to Lesson 14, what's the risk of a candidate still presenting the integration diagram at minute forty of a sixty-minute session?
options: The panel fails the candidate automatically at that mark
It eats into the budgeted Q&A time, which needs real room to breathe
Integration diagrams can't legally be shown after minute thirty
Nothing — pacing doesn't matter as long as content is covered
questions.explain: Running long on the walkthrough directly eats into the Q&A period, which is where a design actually gets tested — losing that time costs more than finishing the walkthrough on time would gain.

questions.prompt: What is "responsive whiteboarding," per Lesson 14?
options: Redrawing a prepared diagram exactly as shown on a slide
Having the panel draw the diagram instead of the candidate
Live drawing used specifically to answer an unplanned question or build something the panel hasn't already seen
Only using a whiteboard app, never a physical whiteboard
questions.explain: Responsive whiteboarding earns its place by showing real-time reasoning on something unplanned, not by redisplaying prepared material the panel could have seen in seconds on a slide.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about the three objection-pattern families from Lessons 15–17.
options: Data/security objections often probe a trade-off between competing protections, like encryption strength versus filterability
Integration/scale objections test whether a design number was actually reasoned through or just guessed
Delivery/governance objections typically reward a clever, scenario-specific answer over a standard, well-documented one
A strong failure-path answer treats the integration's failure mode as a first-class design decision, not an afterthought
questions.explain: Delivery/governance objections reward the boring, standard, well-documented answer over a clever one — "clever and fragile" is a worse governance outcome than "standard and maintainable," which is the opposite of what this option claims.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: Lesson 17 recommends a ________ development model, where all metadata changes flow through a single tracked, version-controlled repository, as the standard answer to governance objections.
questions.explain: A source-driven model gives each environment a traceable, version-controlled source of truth, avoiding uncoordinated changes colliding in production.

questions.prompt: Match each rubric category from Lesson 20 to the question it asks.
right: Did the walkthrough leave genuine room for Q&A?
Did the presentation cover every architecture domain the scenario actually touches?
Did each major decision have a stated, explainable reason?
Did the walkthrough read as one connected story?
questions.explain: Breadth checks domain coverage, Defensibility checks whether decisions had stated reasons, Communication checks narrative connectedness, and Time management checks whether Q&A time was protected.

questions.prompt: Put these steps of the model-answer pattern for handling a panel objection in the order Lessons 15–17 teach them.
items: Recognize which objection-pattern family the question belongs to
Restate the specific trade-off or reasoning already built into the original design
Name the consequence or mitigation if the concern is valid
Land on an answer consistent with the design already presented
questions.explain: Strong answers recognize the objection's shape, restate the design's existing reasoning rather than inventing something new, name the real consequence or mitigation, and stay consistent with what was already presented.

questions.prompt: Why does Lesson 18's second mock session ask candidates to choose a case study they haven't already presented in Lesson 8?
options: Because each case study can only legally be presented once
Because Lesson 8's case studies are no longer valid
Because a fresh scenario is always technically easier
Because drilling the same scenario twice teaches performing it well, not applying the method freshly, which is the actual skill being tested
questions.explain: The point of the exercise is testing the method on unfamiliar material — already knowing a scenario's constraints removes the actual challenge of extracting and applying them fresh.

questions.prompt: What belongs in a portfolio entry per Lesson 19, and what doesn't?
options: A compact summary of reasoning (constraints, assumptions, top risks, blueprint bullets, rejected alternatives), with anything that wouldn't speed up future retrieval cut by the removal test
A full transcript of every mock-session Q&A exchange, since completeness matters most
Only the final diagrams, with no written reasoning at all
A new scenario invented specifically for the portfolio, not material from course labs
questions.explain: A useful entry is short enough to review in a few minutes — a summary of the reasoning, not a transcript of everything ever written about the case study.

questions.prompt: What does this course's wrap-up (Lesson 21) say about carrying the portfolio forward after the course ends?
options: It should be deleted since the course is complete
It should be carried forward and reused for future interviews, review boards, and reference
It should be submitted to Salesforce for certification credit
It should be rebuilt from scratch for every new course
questions.explain: The portfolio is built specifically to be reused, not retired the moment the course ends — its value continues into real interviews and engagements.

questions.prompt: Select every case-study-to-domain pairing below that is correct, per this course's seven case studies.
options: Alder Trust Bank — Financial Services Cloud data model and segregation of duties
Carrow Equipment — territory-based partner sharing and Salesforce Connect
Nimbus Mobile — FERPA-driven advising sharing defaults
Fenwick State University — EDA relationship model and system-of-record split with the SIS
questions.explain: FERPA-driven advising sharing defaults belong to Fenwick State University, not Nimbus Mobile — Nimbus Mobile's case study centers on Omni-Channel routing, event-driven outage alerts, and tiered storage for scale.

questions.prompt: Per Lesson 16, what does a strong answer to a scale-assumption objection (e.g., "what if volume is triple what you assumed") show, rather than insisting the original number was correct?
options: That the entire design would need to be scrapped and rebuilt
That the panel's question is invalid and shouldn't be asked
That the design degrades gracefully — for example by tuning a threshold — rather than breaking entirely if the assumption is wrong
That scale assumptions never actually matter in a real design
questions.explain: A strong answer names the assumption's consequence and shows the design has headroom or a known next step, rather than breaking entirely or insisting the original number was definitely right.
